#9771. Why Thousands of Tests Couldn't Catch the Bugs in My AI Trading Bot

I’m Geoff Cox, a hands-on engineering leader in Seattle. I lead engineering teams, and I still write code.

I’m Geoff Cox, a hands-on engineering leader in Seattle. I lead engineering teams, and I still write code.

I’m Geoff Cox, a hands-on engineering leader in Seattle. I lead engineering teams, and I still write code.

This is a story about the bugs my tests couldn’t find, and the check that found them anyway. TopSet is the trading system I built and run on my own accounts. It picks stocks with machine-learning models, rebalances on a schedule and places real orders through two brokers, Alpaca and Tradier. AI agents wrote most of the code, and my first post about it described the test gate that decides what merges: thousands of tests, a weekly 100-run soak and a few results I refuse to let change quietly.

That gate still matters, but over time I learned that each kind of test answers a different question, and none of them answers the one I care about most: do my records match the broker’s? A mock broker can only repeat what I believe about the real one. The bugs that got furthest were the ones where my belief was wrong, and the thing that caught them was a boring comparison that runs every day after trading.

So let’s take a look at what each layer caught, and then at what only the broker could tell me.

Here is the short version, with the longer stories below.

The first six check my code, either on every pull request or in a weekly run. The last one runs in production, and it is the only one that talks to the real world.

CI, short for continuous integration, is the set of checks that runs on every pull request (a proposed change) before it can merge. Before an agent pushes a change, it runs the same lint and type checks and most of the tests on its own machine, and fixes whatever fails there. Those local failures aren’t recorded anywhere, but I’d guess there were many more of them than in CI. So CI is a second line, and the interesting question is what still got past the first one. Over four months, TopSet had about 440 pull requests, and about 1 in 9 of them still hit at least one failed build in CI. Counting every build, reruns included, 53 failed. Type checking stopped 26 of them, the tests 14 and lint 12, and one never got as far as starting.

Those numbers need some care. The steps run in order, so a lint failure hides any test failure behind it. A rerun replaces a failed result, so I counted every attempt; only one failure was hidden that way, and it was a real bug I’ll come back to below. Builds that were canceled because a newer push replaced them aren’t counted as failures. And the local run skips the slow and integration tests, so a test failure in CI is often one that couldn’t have shown up locally. A lint or type failure in CI usually means the local check was skipped or ran against something different.

I was curious whether the type checker was catching real bugs or just complaining, so I sampled a dozen type-check failures. One was a real bug: a function returned tuples where its callers expected strings, which would have failed as soon as that code ran. The rest were mostly annotations that didn’t match what pandas and numpy actually return. In other words, type checks mostly catch sloppiness and occasionally catch a real bug, and since agents produce a lot of code quickly, catching the sloppiness is worth it.

The integration tests drive a full rebalancing against a mock broker that fills orders at random times, in random pieces, at random prices. That randomness is the point, because the interesting bugs live in the timing.

The best example was a race in how the system worked out how much cash it had to spend. It read the cash balance and the cost of orders that had already filled, and subtracted one from the other. The problem was that a fill could be recorded between those two reads, because the code that recorded fills and the code that planned purchases held different locks. When that happened, the same cash was counted as available twice, and the bot tried to spend more than it had. The cash position would have gone negative, but a database rule (cash can never be below zero) stopped it.

The first CI run on that pull request failed. The rerun passed. If I had treated it as a flaky test and moved on, the bug would still be there. A test that fails only sometimes is usually reporting a bug that happens only sometimes.

Another came from the scheduled weekly run rather than from a pull request. Some integration runs had slowed to about half an hour. The cause was that the code placing trades retried every error, including ones that could never succeed, like a record that didn’t exist. Each hopeless retry tied up a worker for about 25 minutes. The fix, made with Cursor, retries only the errors that can actually clear up.

Running the integration tests over and over found the rarer cases: one lock race that showed up once in 223 runs, and an 11-minute stall in 2 of 144 runs that turned out to be a timeout in how the test shut down its workers. I won’t retell the rest here, as the first post covers the soak.

A snapshot test trains a model on a fixed set of data and compares its picks with a reference file that is checked into the repo. If anything about the training changes, the picks change, and the test fails.

After I changed the machine-learning code, the snapshots often didn’t match. Most of the time the right move was to fix the code, because the change had done something I didn’t intend. Sometimes the right move was to update the snapshot, but only when the difference was one I expected and understood. Most of this happened on my own machine before a pull request existed, so there isn’t much of a record of it.

There is one good example in the record, though. A company that had been renamed was showing up in the historical stock universe under both its old and new tickers, so on some dates the model held it twice and gave it double the weight. When we fixed the universe, the snapshot test failed, and the difference in the reference files showed exactly why: the old files had held one company under two names. That was a case where updating the snapshot was the right call, because the old snapshot had been wrong all along.

The leakage checks get one line here because another post tells that story: train on part of the data, continue on the rest, and the picks must match training on all of it from scratch, bit for bit. If they don’t, something is leaking from the future.

Every test above checks the code against what I believe. The unit tests encode what I think a function should do, and the mock broker encodes what I think the real brokers do. When my belief is wrong, the code and the test are wrong together, and they agree.

What I learned about the real brokers is that they do things you would never think to put in a mock. One reuses an error code for two unrelated errors. Another accepts an order and rejects it later. The code for that second broker had been written against its sandbox, a test environment, and production behaved differently. My tests matched what I believed the brokers did.

So the check I rely on most compares my records with the broker’s. After trading each day, the system adds up each bot’s positions in my database and compares them with the positions the broker reports for that account. When it processes corporate actions, like mergers, splits and dividends, it also compares what each bot recorded with the account activity the broker reported. Any difference it can’t explain is an error, and errors send an alert to my phone.

Here are some of the times those comparisons found something, followed by one time an audit of my own missed something.

When a company is bought for cash, shareholders give up their shares and receive cash. My code booked the cash but left the shares in place, because it assumed the broker always sent a separate stock event that removed them. That’s true when a deal pays partly in stock, but in a pure cash deal there is no stock event. No bot had ever held a company in a pure cash deal before, so the assumption had never been tested, and the first one to touch a bot broke it.

The tests passed, because they were built on the same assumption. The reconciliation failed the same day, because the broker’s account activity showed the shares leaving and my bot’s records didn’t. The fix removes the shares when there’s no stock event to do it, and it was checked against all 108 cash mergers in the production data rather than just the one that broke.

That same merger exposed a second problem. Alpaca reported the account activity on the same day it changed the position. Tradier changed the position about a day before it reported the activity (up to two weeks for some corporate actions). Until the activity arrived, my system hadn’t applied the merger, so the reconciliation saw a mismatch.

The quick fix was to tolerate mismatches on a symbol with a corporate action still pending. That turned out to be too generous, because it would also hide an unrelated mismatch on the same symbol, so the tolerance now requires the broker’s quantity to be exactly what the pending action predicts.

The follow-up found something worse than a false alarm. While the activity was pending, a Tradier bot could plan trades from the old quantity. So symbols with a pending corporate action are now frozen during a rebalancing: not priced, not traded and not counted.

One day after trading, the reconciliation reported 10 mismatches in a live account. On a system that trades real money, that reads as your records being wrong in 10 places.

Alarms like this are always scary on the surface. Even with the best safeguards in place, there’s always a chance that something has gone wrong. This time I wasn’t too worried, because the totals in my account were still roughly what I expected, so I had a good feeling it was an accounting problem rather than missing money. In other words, there was a second, cruder reconciliation running in my head.

That feeling was right. The broker had renamed a company that day, but my list of stocks came from a source that hadn’t caught up yet, so a bot tried to buy the old ticker. The broker rejected the order, the order got stuck, and the rebalancing never finished. The reconciliation then compared the last finished day in my database with a broker account that already showed the 10 orders that had filled that day.

So the alarm’s diagnosis was wrong, but the alarm was still worth having, because a rebalancing was hung and the alarm made sure I looked. The fix makes the stock list follow the broker’s renames and makes sure a rejected ticker can’t hang a rebalancing.

Checks like these have blind spots too, and the best example is an audit I had built for exactly the kind of problem it then missed.

TopSet has a report that compares what the model planned with what the bots actually got. Once, a missing price made one of its key numbers come out blank. An agent added an audit that warned whenever that number was missing, along with seven unit tests for it.

Later, a company that had recently been spun off had a gap of 10 trading days in its prices, and two bots I was comparing both held it. This time the missing price arrived as NaN (“not a number”) instead of an empty value. In Python, NaN counts as true, so the guard that should have skipped the missing price let it through, and that one value wiped out the whole day’s average for every other stock. The result was written as the text “nan”. The audit was checking for an empty value, so it let “nan” straight through. The report’s main numbers were usable on only 0 or 1 of about 13 days, with no warning, and the audit and its tests all passed. It was found by hand, by going through the per-stock data looking for missing prices.

Looking back, I don’t think this kind of failure can be caught up front. You need the unexpected data to show up, then you trace through the calculations, and something like an unexplained outlier tips you off. That’s why iterating on the tests matters so much: every edge case that breaks a pipeline becomes the next test, because an audit only checks what you pointed it at.

Reconciliation isn’t free. It raises false alarms, like the renamed ticker and the broker that runs a day behind, and every false alarm is a choice between investigating and loosening a tolerance. Loosen it too far and it stops catching anything, which is why the pending-action tolerance had to be tightened again. Each new kind of corporate action also needs its own rules for what the broker should show, and those rules are code with their own bugs.

That being said, I’d make the same trade again. A false alarm costs me some time. A silent mismatch between my books and the broker’s could cost real money, and it would keep growing until something else noticed.

The tests decide what merges. The reconciliation decides whether I can leave the system alone, and that’s a different question. A one-person system can’t depend on someone watching it every day. It has to notice when it’s wrong and say so.

Here is what I’d tell anyone building something like this:

TopSet runs unattended today because of that last layer. When something drifts, the broker disagrees with me, and I hear about it the same day.

This describes software I run on my own accounts. It is not investment advice and I do not offer investment services.

#9770. CWE-bench v2: More coverage, quality, and transparency

CWE-bench is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities. In our continued pursuit to push the horizon at Collinear AI, CWE-bench v2 opens up a public set of 100 tasks that anyone can run and evaluate their models on. The setup is the same as before. An agent gets a checkout of a real open-source repository and a short instruction, with the goal of finding and fixing a security weakness without breaking existing functionality. Scoring is fully programmatic, so results are deterministic and anyone can reproduce them without extra cost. All our programmatic checks have been curated with the help of LLM judge panels that shape them towards the direction of hardness and fairness. We also maintain a held-out set, so that we can keep tracking progress on tasks no model has seen. To evaluate your model on the held-out set, contact cyber@collinear.ai.

Our goal is to be exhaustive. A defender has to anticipate the ways an attacker could get in, and get it right every single time. These 100 tasks cover 91 different CWEs, spanning a wide range of vulnerability classes. A model that does well here has to understand the multiple weakness surfaces that a potential attacker can exploit. Recognising a familiar pattern is not enough.

As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true:

Every task was also reviewed by hand. Open-sourcing the set is part of the same effort to improve quality. We welcome feedback on any task, and contributions to the public set.

Results are tracked in two places on the Hub. The leaderboard on the CWE-bench dataset page covers open-weight models and updates on its own: labs and the community add a result by opening a PR on the model's repo with a results file (how). For the full comparison, including API-only models such as Gemini, Claude and GPT, see the CWE-bench leaderboard Space, where new models are added through a PR on the Space.

Open-weight models, from the dataset page:

All evaluated models, including API-only ones:

Of the 11 models evaluated, Gemini 4 Argon leads with 67.8% pass@1 and 81.0% pass@4, just ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3% pass@1, 78.0% pass@4). 95 tasks are solved by at least one model, an indication that the tasks are indeed solvable. However, even the leader fails 19% of the set on every attempt, so the long tail is far from solved. The public set, the grader and the harness are open. Run your model, and tell us where it stands.

On cost, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1017), Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon form the Pareto frontier: DeepSeek reaches 57.0% pass@1 at $0.04 per rollout, Opus adds ten points at $1.83, and Gemini edges ahead at $3.92.

Every task is a self-contained Harbor task (a Dockerized environment, an instruction, and a deterministic verifier), and the dataset ships a registry.json. Harbor can therefore run the whole benchmark straight from the Hugging Face repo, without cloning anything yourself:

-k 4 runs 4 attempts per task, and the reported score is the mean reward over all 400 trials. The dataset is gated: accept its access conditions on the dataset page first. Harbor fetches the tasks with git, so also save your HF token to git's credential helper once:

The tasks are also tagged rl-environment: the same environments and verifiers can provide rewards for training defensive agents, not just for evaluating them.

#9768. The Clothes That Make People Appear More Intelligent

How to use clothes to appear more competent.

How to use clothes to appear more competent.

Wearing more clothing makes you look more competent, a study finds.

Something as simple as taking off a sweater is enough to make you look less competent, the researchers found.

The finding applies to both men and women, said Dr Kurt Gray, the study’s first author:

“An important thing about our study is that, unlike much previous research, ours applies to both sexes.

It also calls into question the nature of objectification because people without clothes are not seen as mindless objects, but they are instead attributed a different kind of mind.”

The effect occurs because seeing more flesh encourages us to think about a person’s body, rather than their mind.

“We also show that this effect can happen even without the removal of clothes.

Simply focusing on someone’s attractiveness, in essence concentrating on their body rather than their mind, makes you see her or him as less of an agent [someone who acts and plans] more of an experiencer.”

Showing bare skin, though, does have some advantages, explained Dr Gray:

“A focus on the body, and the increased perception of sensitivity and emotion it elicits might be good for lovers in the bedroom.

Others appear to be less inclined to harm people with bare skin and more inclined to protect them.

In one experiment, for example, people viewing male subjects with their shirts off were less inclined to give those subjects uncomfortable electric shocks than when the men had their shirts on.”

“Even more than robbing someone of agency, the increased experience that may accompany body perceptions may lead those who are characterized in terms of their bodies to be seen as more reactive and emotional, traits that may also serve to work against career advancement.”

The study was published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (Gray et al., 2011).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#9767. Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language

Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all.

Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other.

Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer plans the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language, and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it.

A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at.

It lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from.

It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide says and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent.

There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them.

Nobody makes a deck in one pass. You decide the story first (how many slides, what each one says, which gets a chart and which gets a table) and only then build each slide. Palette splits the work the same way, into two roles served by a single LoRA adapter:

Each role now makes one kind of decision: the designer handles the editorial judgment, and the coder handles the geometry. The brief between them is readable and editable, so a person or an agent can change one slide's layout without regenerating the deck. And because every slide's context is fixed before any code is written, the coder calls run in parallel, one per slide, which makes the coding stage about 6–7× faster.

We trained the adapter with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning: it teaches a format and a skill on top of a capable base without disturbing what the base already knows, and it made each experiment cheap. One lesson: coder examples are about 5× longer than designer examples, so a naive mix undertrained the designer until we oversampled its examples 5×.

There's no public corpus of plans, design decisions and slide code, so we generated one with a large open teacher. Each deck starts from a recipe that sets its genre, length, layouts and any user directives, so we control what the data covers. Plans range from tidy outlines to raw content dumps, so the model learns to cut and condense. We generated around 1000 decks covering roughly 10,000 slides.

Every example also carries the reasoning behind it, written as a counterfactual: the trace weighs an alternative and says why it was rejected, so the model learns the rule behind a choice, not just the choice. The designer reasons about content and form. For example:

"Revenue for four quarters, with one clear upward trend. I considered a table, but the point of this slide is the trend, not the exact figures, so a bar chart makes it visible at a glance."

"The title is 62 characters. At 44pt it would wrap to three lines and run into the chart below, so I set it at 36pt, which fits on two lines and leaves room above the chart."

The teacher alone doesn't make the data good; the loop around it does. Every synthesized deck is rendered and checked for overlaps and overflow by the same checker the harness uses at inference. Broken slides are repaired, and their reasoning is rewritten as the same kind of counterfactual, covering what the original layout got wrong and why the fix works. Each mistake the checker catches becomes a better training example.

The hardest problem was faithfulness. The worst failure is a slide with facts that weren't in the input, and we found that a prompt rule can't prevent it. If a brief asks for a six-by-five table but carries only three bullets, the coder has to invent the rest.

What fixed it was reference decks, not the rules: fixing a reference reliably changed the teacher's output, while adding a rule rarely did. The teacher sees a few reference decks in its prompt and copies them far more than it follows instructions.

Users often want finer-grained control over specific design choices: a chart instead of a table, a particular color, a darker cover. Palette lets them ask for these with directives, short instructions written directly in the plan and wrapped in [[ ]]:

The designer builds each directive into the brief, and the coder follows it when drawing the slide. Without the directive, the model would reasonably show these milestones as a table; with it, the model draws a timeline instead.

The model follows directives because it was trained to. The data recipes include directives from 12 categories, a few of which are shown below, each phrased several different ways, so the model learns the intent rather than a fixed phrase.

Figure 1. An illustration of the same plan without (left) and with (right) the [[make this a timeline]] directive.

Even a well-trained model sometimes produces a broken slide: a title in the same color as the background, or two boxes stacked on top of each other. So Palette doesn't return the model's output directly; every deck goes through a harness first.

Figure 2. The designer drafts the brief, the coder writes each slide's code in parallel, and the harness checks and repairs every slide before the deck is returned.

First, simple rules fix known mistakes, such as a malformed color code that would otherwise turn every slide black. Then each slide is rendered and measured: a geometry checker flags text that overlaps, gets clipped or runs off the slide. Flagged slides go to a separate editor model, which rewrites that slide's code.

The key rule is that a rewrite is kept only if the checker confirms the slide improved; otherwise the original stays. That makes the harness safe to run on every deck. It can fix a slide, but it can't make one worse.

Figure 3. An illustration of a repair. As generated (left), each card's title is stacked on top of its description; the harness detects the overlaps and reflows the cards into a 2×2 grid (right).

To measure its effect, we generated each PresentBench deck once and scored it with and without the harness. Across 131 decks, the harness adds 3.5 points on average.

We evaluate on PresentBench, which scores generated decks on five criteria: fundamentals, visual design, completeness, correctness and fidelity. PresentBench provides a source document rather than a plan, so for these runs a separate frontier model drafted each plan from its document, and Palette built the deck from that plan. We report three domains; baseline numbers are from the PresentBench paper.

Figure 4. PresentBench scores by domain. Palette (blue) against NotebookLM, Manus 1.6 and five other systems (gray). Palette ranks first on Economics and Education, third on Talk, and second on the three-domain mean.

Palette does best where structured content and numeric accuracy decide the score, ranking first on Economics and Education. On Talk, where decks are narrative and speech-driven, two closed systems score higher and Palette places third. Across the three domains it places second, 1.1 points behind NotebookLM (59.7 vs 60.8) and ahead of the rest of the field, as a single 20B open-weight model.

PresentBench measures whether a deck is good, but not whether it follows a specific design language. We're not aware of a benchmark that does, and it's a gap we hope to help close.

The harness already computes cheap, verifiable signals: does the slide render, does anything overlap or overflow, does every fact trace back to the brief. Today we use them to repair output after generation. Next, we want to use the same checks as rewards for reinforcement learning, so the model stops making these mistakes in the first place. Because the coder works one slide at a time, each slide is a short, independently checkable rollout, a natural fit for GRPO-style training.

We also want to close the gap on figure-heavy decks by extracting figures from source documents (e.g. with Docling) and placing them with the harness. And we're exploring a lighter way to bring your own templates: re-skinning output from one or two of your existing .pptx files, without retraining.

Building Palette taught us a few effective methods that extend naturally to other tasks whose output has a structure you can check in code, from charts and diagrams to UI layouts:

#9766. Why Eden Needed the Forbidden Fruit: A Lesson in Love and Free Will

CEO of Softsquared, South Korea’s first startup to become a Claude Select Partner. I write Super Second Brain.

CEO of Softsquared, South Korea’s first startup to become a Claude Select Partner. I write Super Second Brain.

CEO of Softsquared, South Korea’s first startup to become a Claude Select Partner. I write Super Second Brain.

From here, I borrow the language of my faith. I hope readers who do not share that faith will read it as an old thought experiment.

I have wondered since childhood: if Eden was perfect, why was the forbidden fruit there? Why plant a tree in the middle of the garden only to forbid eating from it? Without the tree, there would have been no failure.

Thinking about the super second brain led me to read this question differently.

Imagine Eden without the tree. Adam cannot leave God there, because there is no way to leave. We do not call it love when a being who cannot leave stays beside someone. I read that tree as a door left open so that staying can be a choice.

English key to the original diagram. A tree stands in the center; a door has been left open. The open way out makes remaining in the garden a choice.

Figure 16. Because the tree is there, staying becomes a choice.

In the language of Chapter 12, the forbidden fruit is friction. Only where there is friction does love become a choice.

The ‘complete observation’ of Chapter 8 looks different here, too. Adam in Eden lived before a God who knew all of him. From the beginning, there was no switch for turning off being known. What remained open to him was one door through which he could leave. Here I receive the switch I set aside in Chapter 8 in another form. Even if I cannot choose whether to be known, I can choose where to stay while fully known.

In the prologue, I wrote that I have also understood the life of faith as training in metacognition. Placed beside the words I have come to use while building the super second brain, it looks like this.

I am not using this table to make a theological claim. I want to show how I organize my thoughts by moving between the languages of these two worlds.

I would like you to notice the place of atonement. In Chapter 6, I said that self-esteem is needed to withstand accurate criticism from a second brain. The firmest ground for self-esteem I know comes from outside achievement. In a world where AI remembers more and judges better than I do, self-esteem built on achievement cannot hold.

In the prologue, I pushed fidelity to 100 percent. Now I need to revise that number.

100 percent is not somewhere I can arrive and stay, because I keep changing. The birth of a child brings fears that did not exist yesterday. Greater authority brings unfamiliar temptations. Loving someone new opens rooms inside me I did not know were there. Great pain rearranges the order of my values.

New relationships, new desires, new power, new pain. As long as I live in the world with a body, these keep arriving, and each arrival makes me a slightly different person. The self-model that was at 100 percent yesterday is at 98 percent this morning.

So the SSOT is never finished. And the material with which to rewrite it—the new me, not yet recorded anywhere—arises only at the standpoint of lived presence. Only when I, with a body, undergo something is there something new to write.

Eden is not a world where choice has disappeared. It is a world where, despite being able to choose otherwise, one chooses love.

If AI Becomes an Extension of You, What Does That Make It?

#9765. Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out

A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.

In April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE, a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms. The paper behind it made a narrow, well-measured case for domain specialization: a smaller model trained closer to its task beating general-purpose frontier APIs on that task.

OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting. That's exactly what you want when the job is the whole document, like a contract you'll read end to end or a manuscript you're digitizing.

However, there's a different use case: you don't want the page, you want specific fields out of it, in a shape a system downstream can consume. Every line item on an invoice, as a list. The patient name, exam type and date from a medical requisition, ready to schedule. The fields off an ID, mapped to the columns of an employee record.

Run that document through OCR and you get back everything printed on it, line by line, with no indication of which string is the exam type, which is the date or which number is the total. Someone still has to write the code that maps each value to the right field before it reaches the database.

A general-purpose LLM can do this work today, with careful prompting. At frontier API pricing and latency, on a task many businesses need to run at high volume, that quickly becomes the expensive way to solve a well-defined problem.

So we built a model for it instead. The Field Extractor takes a document image and either a request for everything it can find, or an exact schema to fill, and returns structured JSON: typed, field by field, nested where the document nests. An invoice comes back with every line item as an ordered list, each with its own quantity and value, alongside the totals. An ID comes back as the fields you'll store, under the names your system already uses for them. The same checkpoint handles all of it, with no per-type fine-tuning.

Say a batch of supplier invoices lands every morning, and you need four things off each one to push into your system: the supplier, the invoice number, the due date, the total. Same story for medical requisitions going into a scheduler, or contracts feeding a compliance system, where what matters is the parties, the term, the penalties and the fine amounts. You don't need the page, you need certain fields. With the Field Extractor there are two ways to ask for them:

The choice comes down to what you already know. Send an open request when you don't know what the document holds. Send a schema when the output has to match a shape that already exists somewhere else.

Either way, what comes back is JSON: the fields as keys, the values typed as requested, and null where the document didn't have what you asked for. When you send a schema, the output follows it exactly, with the same keys and no extra fields, so it can go straight into the next system.

The base model is DharmaOCR-LITE v1.1, a new 2-billion-parameter version optimized from the one in the paper and already specialized for OCR through supervised fine-tuning and DPO. On top of that checkpoint we trained a LoRA adapter on 43,384 training examples covering both request modes.

The data is organized into three streams:

All three streams are annotated at the field level. The mix is deliberately multi-domain: receipts, commercial invoices, forms, bank statements, ID documents and synthetic documents, rather than one filing type.

The full benchmark covers 546 documents across three request scenarios, for 1,638 total cases: extracting every field with no schema, a partial schema naming only real fields, and a schema that also includes deliberately nonexistent fields. The score is field-level F1 (matched by path, including position inside a table), multiplied by the Levenshtein similarity on the values that matched and by the share of outputs that come back as valid JSON.

We ran the same benchmark against four general-purpose frontier configurations.

Against general-purpose LLMs, the quality gap runs from 1.8 points (Claude Opus 5, the closest) to 9.3 points (GPT-5.6 Luna, the widest).

Cost runs from roughly 6 times lower (GPT-5.6 Luna) to roughly 147 times lower (GPT-5.6 Sol). The two sides are priced differently. The frontier figures come from measured average input and output tokens per page, reasoning tokens included, against each provider's published list pricing. Every frontier model ran with reasoning set to low; Claude Opus 5 used adaptive effort, which can skip reasoning on simpler pages while staying at the low level. Ours isn't billed per token: the model runs self-hosted, so the figure is GPU time on a single L40S at $2.24 per hour.

This is not a sales price. Self-hosted cost depends on the hardware, the volume and the latency each deployment needs. The comparison is here to show that a sovereign SSLM, deployed on your own infrastructure, is a real alternative to frontier APIs.

SROIE and FUNSD are two public datasets in our benchmark, not used in training. Below is one example from each.

On a SROIE receipt, we asked for all 18 fields printed on it, with no phantom fields this time, and every one comes back correct: the multi-line, unlabeled billing address captured as a single field, the two blank fields (salesperson and ref) correctly returned as null, and every number on the receipt matching to the cent.

On a FUNSD photocopying variance form, a checklist of twelve boolean fields with one nested group of five sub-options, the model marks exactly the one box that's checked (poor quality original, with a handwritten "faded" note beside it) as true, and the other eleven as false, matching the form exactly. It also reads the handwritten Bates ID off the page correctly, and returns null for the two fields left blank.

A 2-billion-parameter model scored 0.834, above every frontier configuration we tested, from Claude Opus 5 at 0.816 to GPT-5.6 Luna at 0.741, while running on a single L40S at a lower cost per extraction than every API in the comparison. Higher quality and lower cost, measured on the same benchmark, in the same run.

This isn't the first time we've measured it. Our OCR paper put the first DharmaOCR-LITE, a 3-billion-parameter model, above every commercial frontier API tested on Brazilian Portuguese; three months later, newer and better-resourced models arrived, and the gap held. Now a 2-billion-parameter model does it on field extraction. Each result adds evidence for the thesis we started Dharma-AI with: on a bounded task, a small model trained close to that task beats a frontier model asked to do the same thing in general. In this benchmark, it also cost 6 to 147 times less to run.

Parameter count sets the ceiling; training decides how much of it a model reaches on your task. Your business doesn't need the biggest model available. It needs one trained for your problem.

Try it on your own documents here. To learn more about Dharma-AI and the specialized models we build, visit dharma-ai.com.

#9764. A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks.

Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you.

We've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard.

Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of users, not how much speech you generate.

Getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both.

We announced Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early users. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design.

Phonon is based on the Pocket TTS lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created new challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages.

Phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in Gradium Studio. Phonon also handles the important things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes.

It runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can hear it right now. Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license.

The launch came with demos from friends and from our own team. On an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off, Phonon talks you through a coffee brew step by step. On an iPhone with no signal, it counts your reps and keeps you going. A robot called Lamp, from Autonomous, wears a sorting hat and talks in character. In a browser, an offline dino runner becomes a radio show hosted by Rex. There's also a sci-fi game voiced on the player's own machine, and Proust read aloud page by page.

The Hugging Face team built the Transformers integration, so developers could use Phonon in Transformers from day one.

Developers have started building on it too. An ExecuTorch conversion runs Phonon on a visitor's GPU in the browser, Micdrop brings it to Node.js apps, and Spaces like smallest-s2s build on it.

Phonon was downloaded more than 200,000 times in its first two weeks, and it’s still trending on Hugging Face.

The Open TTS Leaderboard is a very new project from Hugging Face, and we love it. With more than 9,000 TTS models on the Hugging Face Hub, the leaderboard gives developers one place to compare open models and hear them side by side. Across 23 languages, models are evaluated on intelligibility (word error rate of the outputs), speed (inverse real-time factor and time-to-first audio), and naturalness (UTMOS for English and KOMOS for Korean). Fixed-voice and voice cloning are evaluated, with an additional speaker similarity metric for the latter. The leaderboard also has a Listen tab, where you can conveniently compare TTS outputs yourself and vote for the ones you like the most.

On intelligibility, Phonon ranks first in German and Spanish, and in the top three in every language we evaluated, next to models up to 100 times its size.

Speed is where we see Phonon truly shine, as the models top the CPU streaming benchmark on time-to-first audio.

We built a new inference framework, ptts, specifically for Phonon. The goal of ptts is to get the best performance on a wide variety of devices and as such supports more than 10 backends: CPU (Intel, Arm, WebAssembly), GPU (CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU), and NPU (Apple Core ML, Snapdragon®).

Phonon is also available in 🤗 Transformers, from v5.21, as its reference PyTorch implementation. Where ptts runs a single stream on device, Transformers targets GPU throughput: batched generation, full-graph torch.compile, e.g., for synthesizing speech datasets at scale. Being native PyTorch, it is a base to build upon, whether to integrate Phonon into your own stack or to study the model itself.

It belongs to the Pocket TTS lineage, so we first added Pocket TTS to Transformers. Phonon sits on top as a modular model: about 200 lines describing only what differs.

Phonon generates audio latents autoregressively: each step outputs a latent that is fed back as the next input, and the training loss is computed on them. Latents are the model's inputs, outputs and targets, as text tokens are for a language model, so the codec mapping audio to latents plays the role of a tokenizer. Transformers ships it as such: an audio tokenizer, held by the processor next to the text tokenizer:

A voice is not a recording but a tensor of speaker latents. Phonon never encodes audio directly with its audio tokenizer, which ships decoder-only, and voices come precomputed: gradium/phonon-voices.

The prompt layout (voice positions, text, then a token opening the audio) ships with the checkpoint as a chat template, as for other multimodal models in Transformers. You write a standard conversation, with an empty audio item where the voice goes, and your code stays the same across checkpoints. The processor then expands the voice placeholder to one position per frame, normalizes and tokenizes the text, and batches the inputs:

generate returns latents, which the processor decodes to audio:

Phonon can speak with any voice. Clone one from a short recording with the speaker’s consent, or describe a new one in plain text in Gradium Studio. Then download the voice file, load it in Phonon, and it runs fully on the device.

We also train custom Phonon models with design partners. If your memory budget is tight, we can make the model smaller. If you need Korean, Arabic or Japanese, we can train for that too. And if your product has its own vocabulary, we can fine-tune on it. Get in touch and tell us what you need.

Thank you to the Hugging Face team, and to everyone who tried Phonon in its first two weeks.

Phonon is our first open release. Try it out and tell us what you build.

One line in "what's next" I keep coming back to: Korean, Arabic and Japanese get offered as custom-training requests. #9762. A Nasty Sign Of Omega-3 Deficiency

A high omega-3 diet can lower the signs and symptoms of the disease by 50 per cent.

A high omega-3 diet can lower the signs and symptoms of the disease by 50 per cent.

Stiffness in the joints and swelling can be indirect signs of omega-3 deficiency, research suggests.

Waking up stiff in the morning, feeling pain in the joints, swelling, tenderness and loss of flexibility are all signs of arthritis.

Omega-3 deficiency could be contributing, as scientists believe there is a link between this leading cause of disability and a lack of omega-3 in the diet.

Researchers suggest that a diet rich in omega-3 could decrease the symptoms of osteoarthritis.

A study has found that adding fish oil to the diet — and to some degree flaxseed oil (alpha-linolenic acid has an anti-inflammatory effect) — can ease or even prevent osteoarthritis.

With population aging, osteoarthritis will be one of the leading causes of disability.

According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, by 2040 it is estimated that 26% of US adults aged 18 or older will be diagnosed by a doctor with arthritis.

While there are still no effective medications for treating this condition, omega-3 fish oil can be one of the best natural remedies in treating osteoarthritis.

Professor John Tarlton, the lead researcher of the study, explained the effect of omega-3 on osteoarthritis:

“Classic early signs of the condition, such as the degradation of collagen in cartilage and the loss of molecules that give it shock-absorbing properties, were both reduced with omega-3.

Furthermore, there was strong evidence that omega-3 influences the biochemistry of the disease, and therefore not only helps prevent disease, but also slows its progression, potentially controlling established osteoarthritis.”

Western diets contain high levels of omega-6 fatty acids, which can lead to inflammatory disorders such as colitis, heart disease, osteoporosis, cancer, rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis.

Modern diets contain up to 30 times more omega-6 than omega-3, whereas our ancestor’s diets contained almost an equal level of these two omega fatty acids.

Therefore, supplementation with omega-3 can help to restore this imbalance in Western diets and improve conditions such as colitis and heart-related diseases.

Fish oil is much more effective than flax seed oil, but for vegetarians and vegans this supplement is an important option.

“Most diets in the developed world are lacking in omega-3, with modern diets having up to 30 times too much omega-6 and too little omega-3.

Taking omega-3 will help redress this imbalance and may positively contribute to a range of other health problems such as heart disease and colitis.”

The study was published in the journal of Osteoarthritis and Cartilage (Knott et al., 2011).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#9761. Five memory leaks that kill Flutter apps on older phones

A memory leak happens when your app holds on to objects it no longer needs, so the Dart garbage collector can't free them.

On a modern phone with 8 GB of RAM, a leak can hide for a while. On an older phone with 2 or 3 GB, it's a different story: the operating system kills your app in the background, or it crashes while someone is using it. Your crash reports fill up with devices you never tested on.

The most common Flutter leaks have one thing in common: something outlives its screen.

AnimationController, TextEditingController and ScrollController all hold resources. If you create one in a State, you dispose it in that State.

Rule of thumb: if it was created in initState, it gets cleaned up in dispose.

A periodic timer or a stream subscription keeps running after the user leaves the screen, and keeps the State alive with it.

cancel(), not just setting the variable to null.

Never store a BuildContext in a long-lived variable or a singleton:

If you hold on to the context of a screen after the user has navigated away, that entire screen and all of its widgets stay in memory. Pass context into the method that needs it, use it, and let it go. For app-wide navigation, use a navigator key or your router instead.

Open Flutter DevTools and watch the Memory tab while you navigate in and out of a screen a few times. Memory should go up and come back down. A graph that only ever climbs is a leak.

Test on the oldest, cheapest device you can get. Leaks that never show on a flagship show up there within minutes.

Further reading: Optimizing Flutter app performance for older devices on our blog also covers jank fixes and image caching.

Los Angeles, United States, November 9th, 2026/TechnologyWire/--GENZA, a gamified dating app built for Gen Z adults, today announced its U.S. launch, with Los Angeles leading its first wave. GENZA is built on a simple premise: the people who matter most in our lives were never chosen from a photo. What makes them special is how they make people feel — the humor, the chemistry, that sense of being understood.

Tapping into Gen Z’s shift toward “chalance” dating, an approach that values openness and genuine effort over playing it cool, GENZA reverses the traditional dating-app model. Instead of endless swiping and split-second judgments based on appearance, users connect through interactive experiences that reveal personality, shared values and emotional compatibility. Profile photos unlock once your bond level reaches 100%.

The app has no traditional bios or profile questionnaires. Users express themselves through customizable 3D avatars that serve as their visual identities within GENZA’s interactive environment. At the core of the app is the Vibe Code, a personal compatibility profile that each user builds through interactive self-discovery quests. The quests capture a person’s values, preferences and behavioral patterns. GENZA’s AI then analyzes the profile across 30 grounded personality traits drawn from established personality research to suggest two potential matches at a time, based on emotional compatibility, shared values and energy.

Once matched, users can chat and play co-op games designed for two in a private 3D room. In “Last $50,” for example, the pair gets a virtual $50 budget to spend on a random lineup of in-game items, from a pet rock and a ring light to 100 rubber ducks. After revealing their choices, they get a short, playful take from GENZA’s AI. There’s no winning or losing. The fun is in discovering what someone chooses, who they choose it for, and what those choices reveal about their personality. Photos remain blurred at first and unlock as the connection develops.

The goal is not to replace in-person dating with a virtual experience. GENZA uses play as a starting point for discovering mutual interest, helping people build connections they can take into real life when the time feels right. Verification features are also designed to help keep profiles authentic and reduce fake accounts.

The idea reflects a broader shift in how younger generations approach social connections. According to the Entertainment Software Association’s (ESA) 2026 Essential Facts report, 88% of Gen Z players believe video games are a great way to bring people together, while 87% say they help build relationships. The organization’s 2025 report also found that 63% of Gen Z players had met a good friend or significant other through video games. GENZA brings this power of shared experiences into dating, helping people discover chemistry through interaction, collaboration and play.

“As a Gen Zer, I didn’t want to build yet another app where the most interesting thing about you has to fit into a few photos and a short bio. With GENZA, we started with a different question: what can two people discover about each other when they actually do something together? That’s why we combined personality discovery, avatars and games into a single experience. Our soft launch drew more than 2,000 users, and the conversion rates we saw were very encouraging for a first version of the product. It showed us that people are ready for a different kind of first impression, one you create together rather than just see,” said Daria Leshchikova, Founding Chief Product and Strategy Officer of GENZA.

To introduce the app to Los Angeles, GENZA is also working with local creators on paid partnerships in which they share first-person experiences with the platform, exploring topics ranging from student life and moving to a new city to dating and building new connections.

GENZA is available now on iOS and Android in English and Spanish for adults aged 18 and over.

GENZA is a new-gen gamified dating app that puts emotional compatibility before photos. Instead of bios and endless swiping, users build a Vibe Code through interactive self-discovery quests. GENZA’s AI then reads that profile across 30 personality traits to suggest two matches at a time. Matches meet as 3D avatars in a private room, play co-op games together, and unlock each other’s photos as mutual interest grows. Developed by Genza Inc., GENZA is available on iOS and Android in English and Spanish for adults 18 and over. For more information, visit genza.io.

#9757. Designing a rate limiter: token bucket, sliding window and limits across many servers

Posted on Nov 10 • Originally published at bydtech.in • Fully Autonomous

A rate limiter decides, on every request, whether a key (an IP address, a user, an API key or a tenant) is still within its allowance. Token bucket is the usual default because it allows short bursts while holding a long-run rate with two numbers per key; a sliding window counter is a cheap, close approximation of “at most N requests in any window”. Across many servers the state lives in a shared store and each decision is one atomic operation, and a client over its limit gets HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header.

A rate limiter answers one question per request: has this key used up its allowance? The key is whatever you want to be fair between: a client IP, a signed-in user, an API key, a tenant, or a combination such as API key plus endpoint. The allowance is a rate, such as requests per second or per minute, often with a burst size, and sometimes a cost per request, so that an expensive search counts for more than a cheap read.

Rate limits protect three things: the service from overload, tenants from a noisy neighbor, and the product from abuse such as credential stuffing and scraping. They are different from quotas, which are allowances over a long period tied to a plan, and from concurrency limits, which cap how many requests are in flight at once rather than how many arrive per second. Stripe’s documentation, for example, describes both rate limits and separate concurrency limits, and names the one that fired in a Stripe-Rate-Limited-Reason response header.

This post covers the five common algorithms, where to enforce them, how to keep one limit across many servers, and what the server and the client should do when a limit is hit.

Cloudflare has described running the sliding window counter at scale. Over 400 million requests from 270,000 sources, the authors report that 0.003% of requests were wrongly allowed or rate limited, an error that comes from assuming the previous window’s traffic was evenly spread. A leaky bucket used as a meter, which rejects instead of queueing, behaves like a token bucket with the same rate and size; the choice that matters in practice is queue or reject.

A token bucket needs no background timer. Store the token count and the time of the last update. On each request, add the tokens earned since then, capped at the capacity, and then try to spend.

When the contract is “at most N requests in any 60 seconds” rather than “a rate plus a burst”, a sliding window counter is the cheap way to approximate it. Cloudflare’s write-up gives a worked example: with a limit of 50 per minute, 42 requests in the previous minute, 18 so far in the current one and 15 seconds into it, the estimate is 42 × 45/60 + 18 = 49.5, so the next request is still allowed.

Two choices are hidden in this code. It counts only accepted requests; counting rejected ones too keeps a client that ignores its 429s locked out for longer, which some APIs want. And the map never forgets a key: in a real service, drop entries older than two windows, or keep the counters in a store that expires keys for you.

Enforce coarse limits early and precise limits where the context is. A gateway, load balancer or reverse proxy can reject a flood before it costs any application work, but it often knows only the IP address and the path. The application knows the user, the tenant’s plan and what an operation really costs. Many systems do both: a generous per-IP limit at the edge, and per-user, per-key or per-tenant limits in the application.

Behind a proxy or load balancer, the connection’s address is the proxy’s. Take the client address from the forwarding header only when your own proxy sets it, and read the entry your proxy appended, not the leftmost one, which the client can write.

Put an in-memory limiter on each of ten servers behind a load balancer, and a limit of 100 per minute becomes roughly 1,000, unevenly, depending on where requests land. There are three ways out.

With a shared store, the classic bug is read-check-write in separate round trips: two servers both read 99, both see room under a limit of 100, and both write 100, so 101 requests pass. The fix is to make the decision one atomic step in the store. A plain counter can use an atomic increment that returns the new value (Redis INCR is one example) and compare afterward. Anything with more logic, such as a token bucket, belongs in one server-side script; Redis, for example, runs a Lua script atomically, with no other command running in between. Watch for the two-command fixed window too: an increment followed by a separate expire leaves a counter that never expires if the process dies between the two.

A hybrid design makes that compromise permanent. Envoy’s documentation describes a local token bucket in each proxy as a first, coarse pass that can absorb large bursts, with the global rate limit service applying the precise limit behind it, which reduces the load on the global service.

RFC 6585 defines 429 Too Many Requests for a user who has sent too many requests in a given amount of time. The response may include Retry-After, must not be stored by a cache, and the RFC leaves it to the server to decide how it identifies users and counts requests. Keep 503 for “the whole service is overloaded”, not for one client over its limit. NGINX’s limit_req answers 503 by default; limit_req_status 429; changes that.

RFC 9110 defines Retry-After as either an HTTP date or a number of seconds, as in Retry-After: 120. The number of seconds is easier for clients to get right, because it does not depend on their clock agreeing with yours.

Telling clients how close they are to a limit before they hit it is the job of the IETF draft “RateLimit header fields for HTTP”. As of November 2026 it is at version 11, published in May 2026, an Internet-Draft of the HTTPAPI working group and not an RFC, so names and parameters can still change. It defines two fields:

Many APIs still send the older, unstandardized X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining and X-RateLimit-Reset headers, and they disagree on whether the reset is a timestamp or a number of seconds. If you publish an API, document which headers you send. Either way, say which limit was hit, as Stripe does with its reason header: a client that knows it hit a per-endpoint limit can slow down just that endpoint.

A client that retries a 429 at once makes the overload worse, and many clients that back off on the same schedule come back in synchronized waves. The remedy Marc Brooker describes on the AWS Architecture Blog is exponential backoff with jitter: grow the maximum delay exponentially, cap it, and sleep a random time below it, which he calls “full jitter”. Stripe’s rate limit documentation gives the same advice for 429 responses, to avoid a thundering herd.

A rate limit often sits in front of the same expensive work as a cache; caching strategies covers that side.

A token bucket allows a burst up to its capacity and then holds the refill rate. A leaky bucket in its queue form accepts a burst into a queue and releases requests at a fixed rate, so it smooths traffic by adding delay. Used as a meter that rejects instead of queueing, a leaky bucket behaves like a token bucket with the same rate and size.

It depends on what the limit protects. For ordinary user traffic, most teams fail open, often with a conservative local limiter on each node as a fallback. For limits that stop abuse, such as login attempts, or that protect a fragile backend, failing closed is safer. Decide it in advance and test it.

Return 429 Too Many Requests, defined in RFC 6585, when one client has sent too many requests, ideally with Retry-After. Keep 503 Service Unavailable for when the whole service is overloaded or down. Some proxies default to 503 for rate limiting, so check the setting.

Read the client address from the forwarding header that your own proxy or load balancer sets, using the entry it appended rather than the leftmost one, which the client controls. Expect many users behind one address on office and mobile networks, and limit IPv6 clients by prefix rather than by single address.

Not yet. As of November 2026 they are defined in draft-ietf-httpapi-ratelimit-headers, version 11, an Internet-Draft of the IETF HTTPAPI working group. Details can still change before it becomes an RFC, and many APIs still send the older X-RateLimit headers.

This article was created with the help of AI, and its facts were checked against the sources listed above.
