#9747. Before You Spend More on Ads, Find Out What Happened to Your Last 300 Leads

Founder@ Pinpoint | Marketing Consultant, Fractional CMO | Reduces risks for founders | Marketing grounded into business

Founder@ Pinpoint | Marketing Consultant, Fractional CMO | Reduces risks for founders | Marketing grounded into business

Founder@ Pinpoint | Marketing Consultant, Fractional CMO | Reduces risks for founders | Marketing grounded into business

I worked with a company selling and installing photovoltaic systems for homeowners just as a government subsidy program was preparing to bring a sharp increase in demand. At the time, the business was receiving between 10 and 20 leads a month. The website needed substantial improvements, enquiries came through different channels, and the sales team had no CRM to manage them in one place.

Preparing for the campaigns involved working on the commercial process alongside the marketing activities. The company needed a way to collect enquiries, make them available to sales and keep track of what happened after the first contact. These decisions had to be made while the website, campaigns and sales procedures were being developed.

During the campaign, the company generated approximately 10,000 leads, around 3,300 per month. The government program created exceptional demand, while the advertising campaigns and website improvements helped capture that interest.

My role covered marketing strategy and the coordination of its implementation. I managed the Meta campaigns, coordinated the agency responsible for Google Ads and worked with the web developers on the website. On the commercial side, I worked with the founder and sales team on selecting and integrating the CRM, defining how enquiries would be handled and preparing the information salespeople needed in their conversations.

The volume eventually reached a level that would have been difficult to manage through the previous arrangements. The preparation of the commercial process became an important part of making that increase manageable.

When someone fills in a contact form, the information may pass through several systems before reaching a salesperson. The website receives the submission, an advertising platform may register a conversion, an automation tool transfers the data, and the CRM creates or updates a record.

Each system records a different stage. A successful conversion in the advertising account tells marketing that somebody completed the intended action. The sales team needs the information to appear in the right place, with enough context to understand the enquiry and continue the conversation.

The difference becomes important when the number of requests increases.

At 10 or 20 enquiries a month, a small team may be able to manage follow-up through emails, spreadsheets and direct conversations. People can compensate for an imperfect process because the volume is relatively low. When several hundred requests arrive in a week, keeping track of them requires a shared system and clear responsibilities.

There is also a reporting limitation worth understanding. A CRM can show the records it has received, including their status and assigned owner. An enquiry that disappears before reaching the CRM may be absent from its reports altogether.

For that reason, it is useful to keep a record of submissions at the point where they enter the process, such as the website form or the advertising platform, and compare it with the records created in the CRM. The comparison helps identify requests that were submitted successfully but did not reach the intended destination.

The company also needs a consistent way to distinguish legitimate enquiries from internal tests, spam and duplicates. Otherwise, the numbers can become difficult to reconcile, especially when the same person contacts the business through more than one channel.

These details affect the quality of information available to both marketing and sales. They become increasingly relevant when management is making decisions based on lead volumes and campaign performance.

In the renewable energy project, we brought enquiries from several sources into a common CRM. Website forms, paid campaigns and other communication channels needed to feed into a commercial process that the sales team could use consistently.

Zapier was part of the setup, transferring leads from paid campaigns into the sales workflow. I coordinated the CRM selection and implementation, the integration requirements and the work between the people responsible for the different parts of the process.

Once the enquiries reached the CRM, we also needed to establish how they would be handled.

Who would contact the customer, what information should be available before that conversation and how should the team deal with requests requiring technical clarification? These decisions involved the sales function and had to reflect the company's actual capacity.

The customer questions were also specific to the market situation. Homeowners wanted to understand whether they qualified for the subsidy program, what documentation was required, how the financing worked and what installation involved. A salesperson needed accurate information to explain the process and identify whether an enquiry could become a viable commercial opportunity.

We worked on sales scripts, answers to recurring questions and procedures for handling the incoming requests. We also introduced qualification logic to help the team prioritize enquiries as volumes increased.

The CRM provided a common place for information and follow-up. The value of the setup depended on how the team used it and whether the information reaching sales was sufficient for the next step.

This is an important consideration when selecting software. A company can compare CRM features and automation options extensively, yet still encounter difficulties if the people involved have different expectations about how a request should be handled.

For a business preparing to scale acquisition, the practical requirements deserve attention early in the project. They influence the choice of integrations, the CRM configuration, the procedures used by sales and the information that marketing needs to collect.

Marketing reports provide detailed information about the activities that generate enquiries. Impressions, clicks, conversion rates and cost per lead help evaluate the campaigns and identify areas that need improvement.

Once a person submits a request, the commercial process introduces additional measurements.

I would separate the time needed for an enquiry to reach its assigned owner from the time until the first human contact attempt. The first depends largely on the integrations and routing procedures. The second is influenced by staffing, workload and the way the sales team organizes follow-up.

A record showing that a lead was created in the CRM says little about when somebody actually tried to contact that person. Keeping the two moments separate helps management identify where a delay occurred.

The distinction between an attempted contact and a successful conversation matters as well. The team controls when it makes a call or sends a personal response. Whether the customer answers depends on circumstances outside the team's control.

Response time has been studied in connection with online lead generation for many years. In The Short Life of Online Sales Leads, published in Harvard Business Review in 2011, researchers audited 2,241 US companies by sending test enquiries. They found that 37% responded within an hour, while 23% did not respond at all.

The research provides historical evidence of how frequently online enquiries went unanswered or received delayed responses. For an individual business, current measurements are needed to understand how its own process performs.

Working hours are another part of the calculation. A request submitted on Friday evening may follow a different schedule from one received on Monday morning. The relevant departments should agree on response expectations and apply them consistently.

These measurements are useful when they reflect how customers are actually handled. They can also reveal differences between acquisition channels or periods of unusually high demand.

If a particular form regularly produces records with missing information, the problem may require changes to the form or integration. If leads are assigned correctly but remain untouched for long periods, management may need to examine workload, priorities or sales capacity.

The data gives the teams a common basis for discussing where improvements are needed.

Before increasing the acquisition budget, I would recommend testing the route followed by a real enquiry, using the same forms and channels available to customers.

Submit a request and record when it was sent. Then check when it appeared in the CRM, whether the information was transferred correctly and which person received responsibility for follow-up. The test continues until the first human contact attempt has been recorded.

The timing should be assessed against expectations agreed in advance. For an automatic transfer between systems, a company might initially test a target of a few minutes. Human follow-up needs its own target, taking into account working hours, the type of enquiry and the team's capacity.

Each important source deserves a separate test because the routes can differ. A website form may be connected directly to the CRM, while a paid social lead form may use an automation platform. Email enquiries can require yet another procedure.

After confirming the normal route, I would check several situations that can expose weaknesses in the setup.

A duplicate submission should be recognized without creating unnecessary confusion in the sales process. A request arriving outside working hours should follow the agreed schedule. An enquiry assigned to somebody who is absent should have a way to reach another responsible person.

I would also test the situation in which a customer receives an automatic confirmation, but the request fails to reach the sales team. This is particularly important because the confirmation can give the customer the impression that the process is moving forward.

The purpose of testing these scenarios is to establish how the company identifies a problem, who receives the relevant information and which person or department can resolve it.

A single successful test cannot establish how reliably the process operates under normal conditions. The company also needs to examine records collected during actual activity, particularly when volumes increase.

Together, these checks can show whether the integrations and procedures are functioning as intended and where additional preparation may be necessary.

Consider a business generating 300 enquiries a month and planning to increase its advertising budget substantially.

I would begin by reviewing what happened to those 300 enquiries. How many reached the CRM correctly, received an owner and were contacted within the agreed time? How many became meaningful commercial conversations, and what happened to the remaining requests?

The answers help determine whether the next investment should go primarily toward acquisition or whether the commercial process needs attention first.

A company may discover that the campaigns are generating relevant enquiries, while the sales team has limited capacity to follow up. Additional advertising would then increase the number of requests entering the same process.

In another situation, the handoff may work well, but few enquiries become qualified opportunities. That would justify examining the targeting, the offer, the information collected through forms and the conversations taking place afterward.

These assessments require the teams to look beyond their individual reports.

In the renewable energy project, the rapid growth in demand made coordination with the commercial operation especially important. We worked on the lead-handling process and the materials used by sales while the campaigns and website were being developed. The company also had to adapt its operational capacity as demand increased.

The subsidy program created unusual market conditions, so I would be careful about applying the campaign's numerical results to other businesses. The questions regarding capacity and the commercial process remain relevant whenever management expects a substantial increase in enquiries.

The same reasoning applies to promises made in marketing materials.

A response-time claim, such as a commitment to answer enquiries within an hour, should be supported by measurements showing that the company can achieve it consistently. I prefer to evaluate performance over a meaningful period, including busy weeks and staff absences, before recommending a measurable promise to customers.

Delivery expectations, installation schedules and quotation times deserve similar attention because they depend on several activities within the business.

For acquisition planning, I bring marketing performance, lead handling and sales results into the same management discussion. Each provides information about a different part of the commercial process, and the connections between them can influence the decision to increase spending.

An increase in cost per lead deserves an examination of campaign performance and market conditions. A growing number of uncontacted enquiries calls for a review of the handoff and available sales capacity. When contacts are timely but qualification remains weak, the investigation moves toward the offer, targeting and commercial conversations.

Before recommending a higher acquisition budget, I want to understand how the business handles the enquiries it already receives and what additional volume its people and processes can support. That requires examining what happens after submission, including the requests that have yet to become sales conversations.

#9746. Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan: A Synthetic Dataset Capturing Japan's Demographics and Financial Context

A compound AI approach to Japanese personas grounded in real-world distributions

To address these challenges, Elith and NVIDIA have released Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan, a financial domain extension of the open-source persona dataset "Nemotron-Personas-Japan." To our knowledge, it is the first open persona dataset at million-record scale that pairs Japan’s official statistics with household finance and financial literacy data. Built upon official government statistics, this dataset was developed using NeMo SDG-PGMs, a probabilistic graphical model framework for synthetic data generation (SDG), and NeMo Data Designer, an enterprise synthetic data generation system. Furthermore, to enhance the practical utility of the dataset in financial use cases, it was designed by incorporating insights and feedback provided by leading domestic financial institutions and industry associations, including Sompo Japan, Tokio Marine Holdings, Bank of Fukuoka, Mizuho Financial Group, Meiji Yasuda Life Insurance, and the Financial Data Utilization Association (FDUA).

This dataset expands the environment where Japanese developers and enterprises can develop and evaluate AI tailored to local and industry requirements, without using real customer data. Released under the CC BY 4.0 license, it is available for commercial use. From building conversational agents to customer simulation and model evaluation, it supports practical financial AI development. The Nemotron-Personas collection, including Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan, is designed to seamlessly integrate with the user simulation framework NeMo User Sim, enabling instant execution of simulations drawn from diverse distributions consistent with the real world.

It was built using NVIDIA’s framework for synthetic data generation, NeMo Data Designer. This compound AI system enables complex Jinja templating, Pydantic validation, structured outputs, automated retries, and support for multiple generation backends. This is the essential toolset required for generating such large-scale synthetic datasets. In addition, the following models were utilized:

Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan was designed to align with Japan's official demographic and labor statistics while taking into account key considerations essential for AI training:

Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan is built first for teams creating financial AI in Japan, at banks and insurers and at the startups and integrators that serve them. Each persona carries household finances and financial literacy alongside demographics. Teams can use them to build customer-service agents, evaluate sales conversations/marketing initiatives, run user simulations in NeMo User Sim, and red-team customer-facing AI.

The release also serves anyone building for Japanese users. It holds 9M personas, 50% more than Nemotron-Personas-Japan, across 50 fields instead of 22. That gives any Japanese-language project finer slices of the population to train and test on.

The synthetic personas in this dataset can be leveraged for:

Access to diverse, high-quality training data that reflects real-world populations has long been a challenge in AI development. Enterprise AI development has predominantly relied on private data, creating barriers for researchers, startups, and particularly AI developers in regions with limited available data.

Nemotron-PII-Japan launches the same day. It holds 100,000 synthetic Japanese business documents with labeled personal information, for training and testing detection and redaction models. Its documents are built on Nemotron-Personas-Japan. Use Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan to simulate customers, and Nemotron-PII-Japan to test how your pipeline protects their data.

#9745. 📦 Amazon's Growth Engine: How Convenience, Personalization & Loyalty Drive Repeat Purchases

Imagine two online stores selling the same product at a similar price.

Store A has a confusing checkout, limited delivery information, generic product recommendations, and an unhelpful return process.

Store B makes products easy to discover, offers a smooth checkout, provides reliable delivery information, and remembers what customers may need next.

Which store would you be more likely to visit again?

Most customers don't evaluate an online store only by its product catalog. They also evaluate the effort, confidence, and time required to complete a purchase.

This is where Amazon's growth strategy becomes interesting.

Amazon has built its retail experience around a combination of convenience, personalized discovery, competitive value, customer trust, and loyalty. These elements work together to make shopping easier and give customers reasons to return.

In its 2025 annual report, Amazon identified price, selection, and convenience—including faster shipping—as important contributors to its retail sales growth. Source: Amazon's 2025 Form 10-K

Acquiring a customer creates an opportunity. Delivering a consistently useful experience creates the opportunity for a second, third, and fourth purchase.

Let's break down how Amazon approaches this challenge—and what marketers can learn from it.

Think about the last time you abandoned an online purchase.

Perhaps the checkout required too many steps. Maybe the delivery date wasn't clear, or you couldn't determine whether the product was trustworthy.

Each additional obstacle gives a customer another reason to reconsider.

Amazon's retail experience is designed to reduce many of these obstacles through features such as streamlined purchasing, delivery estimates, order tracking, customer reviews, and simplified reordering.

Its broader strategy emphasizes selection, ease of use, availability, delivery speed, and reliability.

Convenience reduces the effort required to move from intention to action.

Consider a customer who needs laundry detergent.

They don't necessarily want to spend 20 minutes comparing dozens of nearly identical products. They want to find a suitable option, confirm the price and delivery details, and complete the purchase.

If the experience is reliable, buying again can become easier than starting a new search elsewhere.

This creates a potential repeat-purchase advantage.

Saved delivery details, familiar payment options, and streamlined purchasing can reduce unnecessary steps.

Customers should understand when an order is expected to arrive and how they can track it.

Reviews, product specifications, comparisons, and clear return information help shoppers make informed decisions.

Customers buying familiar household essentials benefit from being able to find and reorder products quickly.

A convenient checkout doesn't help much if the product is unavailable or the delivery promise cannot be fulfilled.

Imagine you run an Indian D2C skincare store.

You don't need Amazon's logistics network to improve convenience.

The marketing takeaway: Sometimes the best conversion optimization isn't another advertisement. It's removing the obstacle that prevents an interested customer from buying.

Amazon's catalog is enormous. But showing every customer the same products in the same order would make discovery unnecessarily difficult.

Personalization helps make a large catalog more useful.

Amazon describes using shopping behavior, preferences, and previous interactions to tailor product recommendations and discovery experiences. Its personalized homepage improvements include recommendations based on shopping interests and browsing or purchase history.

For example, someone who recently bought a comforter might see recommendations for matching sheets and pillows.

The point is not simply to show customers more products.

It's to help them discover products that are more relevant to their needs.

Imagine two customers visiting a fashion store.

Customer A frequently browses ethnic wear and festive outfits.

Customer B regularly looks at casual dresses and everyday accessories.

A generic homepage gives both customers the same experience.

A personalized experience could highlight different collections, products, and recommendations based on their interests.

That can make discovery more relevant and create opportunities for additional purchases.

However, personalization must be evaluated with actual customer outcomes. More recommendations do not automatically mean more sales.

Use relevant browsing, search, and purchase signals to understand what customers may be interested in.

Example: Show recently viewed products or relevant category recommendations.

Recommend products that naturally work with an item the customer is considering or has already purchased.

Example: Suggest a compatible phone case after someone buys a smartphone.

Adapt messages to the customer's stage in the journey.

Example: A first-time customer may need onboarding information, while a repeat customer may benefit from relevant new arrivals or replenishment reminders.

These are hypotheses, not guaranteed outcomes. Use experiments to confirm whether the recommendations improve the customer experience and business results.

The marketing takeaway: Personalization works best when it helps customers find something genuinely useful—not when it simply gives them more things to click.

Amazon Prime is one of the clearest examples of Amazon packaging customer benefits into an ongoing membership.

Depending on the country and membership offering, Prime can combine delivery benefits with entertainment and other services.

Instead of asking customers to evaluate every purchase independently, a membership can give them additional reasons to continue shopping within the Amazon ecosystem.

The strategy is not just about offering free delivery.

It's about making the overall membership valuable enough that customers want to keep using it.

A membership may support repeat purchases through several mechanisms:

Amazon's own reporting highlights the role of fast delivery and everyday value in the Prime proposition. Its 2025 Prime delivery update for India reported more than 55 crore products delivered the same or next day to Prime members in India during 2025.

That is an example of how operational convenience can reinforce a membership's perceived value.

You don't need to launch a complicated subscription program.

A smaller business could test a simple loyalty proposition such as:

The important question is whether the benefits motivate incremental customer activity while preserving healthy margins.

A discount that rewards purchases customers would have made anyway can reduce profitability without creating much additional loyalty.

The marketing takeaway: Loyalty programs should reward meaningful customer relationships, not simply subsidize every transaction.

Customers cannot always touch the product, inspect its quality, or speak directly with the person who made it.

They need signals that help them judge whether a product is worth buying.

Amazon's shopping experience includes customer reviews, ratings, product details, and—in supported experiences—summaries of review themes.

These features can help shoppers evaluate products before committing.

Trust affects both the first purchase and the relationship that follows.

A customer who receives a product that matches its description may become more comfortable ordering again.

A customer who encounters misleading information, poor quality, or a difficult refund process may decide to leave—even if the initial purchase was inexpensive.

That means trust isn't just a brand perception metric. It is part of the customer experience.

Don't manipulate reviews or suppress legitimate negative feedback. Authentic criticism can reveal where a business needs to improve.

The marketing takeaway: Your advertising creates expectations. Your product and service experience determine whether customers have a reason to trust those expectations again.

The transaction ends, but the customer's relationship with the product—and potentially the brand—continues.

For some products, the next purchase is predictable. For others, it depends on complementary needs or a new use case.

Amazon's recommendation and shopping experiences can help customers discover related items, while its broader retail model supports recurring purchases across many product categories.

For marketers, this creates two useful opportunities.

Potentially relevant follow-up products could include a laptop sleeve, a compatible mouse, or a suitable adapter.

The key word is relevant. Showing unrelated accessories simply because they have high margins can damage the shopping experience.

Suppose someone buys a product that is consumed over time.

Depending on the product, a reminder or subscription option may be useful when the customer is likely to need another supply.

Replenishment timing should be based on reasonable usage assumptions or customer preferences—not aggressive message frequency.

The exact timing depends on the product. A laptop and a bottle of shampoo should not follow the same replenishment schedule.

The marketing takeaway: The post-purchase journey should help customers get more value from what they bought and make the next purchase easier when a genuine need arises.

It's tempting to attribute Amazon's success to one feature: Prime, recommendations, low prices, or fast delivery.

But the more useful lesson is how these elements reinforce each other.

1. Discovery Relevant products, useful search, and broad selection 2. Conversion Clear information, trust signals, and easy checkout 3. Fulfillment Reliable delivery, tracking, and product experience 4. Retention Useful recommendations, loyalty benefits, and repeat-order convenience 5. Learning loop Use customer behavior and feedback to improve the experience

This is a simplified framework for understanding the strategy, not a claim about Amazon's internal system architecture.

The key idea is that each stage can strengthen or weaken the next.

Relevant recommendations cannot fully compensate for unreliable delivery. Fast delivery cannot fix misleading product information. A loyalty program cannot indefinitely make up for poor quality.

Sustainable repeat purchases depend on the overall experience.

You probably don't have Amazon's logistics network, recommendation infrastructure, or technology budget.

You don't need them to start improving the customer journey.

Start with a focused plan that addresses your biggest source of friction.

Measure conversion rate, checkout abandonment, delivery performance, and refund reasons.

Begin with straightforward, explainable rules.

Measure recommendation conversion, revenue per recipient, and repeat purchase rate.

Identify customers who return naturally, customers who need support, and customers who have become inactive.

Test relevant retention strategies such as:

Measure repeat purchase rate, customer retention, and contribution margin.

Don't assume a new feature has worked just because customers use it.

Run controlled tests where feasible, compare results against a baseline, and check whether improvements are incremental.

Prioritize changes that improve customer value and sustainable profitability.

A good e-commerce dashboard should connect the customer experience to business results.

Definitions can vary depending on the business and reporting system. For example, repeat purchase rate should use a clearly defined customer cohort and observation window.

Imagine a brand launches a loyalty program that increases repeat orders but gives every returning customer a large discount.

Orders may rise while contribution margin falls.

That is why marketers should track both customer behavior and the economics behind it.

The goal isn't simply to maximize the number of orders.

It is to create a better customer experience that supports sustainable, profitable growth.

Here's a practical experiment you could run without building a sophisticated recommendation engine.

Objective: Determine whether a relevant post-purchase recommendation increases repeat or complementary purchases.

Compare the test group with the control group.

Look for incremental purchases, contribution margin, and any negative effects on customer experience. If the sample is too small, treat the result as preliminary rather than declaring a winner.

The test may reveal that personalization works, that a different recommendation is needed, or that customers don't need the follow-up at all.

Amazon's growth model illustrates how convenience, personalization, and loyalty can reinforce one another.

Convenience reduces the effort required to buy.

Personalization helps customers discover relevant products.

Trust makes customers more confident in their decisions.

Loyalty benefits can give customers additional reasons to return.

Post-purchase experiences create opportunities to support customers and meet future needs.

But none of these tactics works in isolation. They depend on a reliable product, a good customer experience, and a business model that can sustain the promises being made.

For marketers, the central lesson is this:

Don't build a growth strategy around getting the customer to buy once. Build an experience that gives the customer a good reason to buy again.

That is the difference between a one-time transaction and a lasting customer relationship.

💬 Your turn: Which factor do you think has the biggest impact on repeat purchases—convenience, personalization, or loyalty programs? Share your reasoning in the comments.

If you enjoyed this breakdown, follow for more practical analyses of growth marketing, e-commerce strategy, customer retention, and marketing analytics.

#9743. How to Scrape Reddit Posts and Comments Without the Reddit API (with Python)

To scrape Reddit without the official API, read Reddit's public pages the way a logged-out visitor does: subreddit feeds, search results, user profiles and post threads. This guide shows how to do that with one API call and get posts, full comment threads, communities and users as clean JSON, with no API key, no OAuth app and no developer account.

This is part 4 of "How my fun projects turned into APIs". Each post takes one side project, explains how it works, and ends with something you can call from your own code. Part 1 covered finding TikTok creator emails, part 2 video transcripts, and part 3 recipes from cooking videos.

Reddit used to be the easiest site on the internet to get data from: add .json to a URL, or register a free API app. That changed:

After three side projects, I had a different problem: I didn't know what to build next. The best ideas usually come from people describing a real problem in their own words, and the place they do that most is Reddit. Posts like "is there a tool that...", "alternative to X" and "I'd pay for something that...".

My plan was simple: search Reddit for those phrases across a few niches, read the threads, and make a list of problems people would pay to solve. Doing that by hand took an evening per niche, and the official API route meant applying for access and waiting.

So I wrote a scraper that reads the same public pages any logged-out visitor sees. First subreddit feeds, then keyword search, then full comment threads, because the best details are always in the replies. Then I added keyword filters to cut the noise, and finally AI tags that mark each post with its pain point, whether the person asks for a recommendation, and whether they say they'd pay.

The list of ideas was useful. The scraper was more useful, so I made it a public API.

The tool is an Apify Actor called Reddit Scraper. It reads Reddit as a logged-out visitor, so it needs no login, no Reddit API key and no OAuth app.

Keyword searches can also return comments, communities and users. Every post can bring its comments, with reply depth and parent ID, so you can rebuild the whole thread.

To get the top posts of a subreddit instead:

Install the client with pip install apify-client, then:

Each row has a dataType: post, comment, community or user. A real post:

This is the part I built the scraper for. Search for phrases people use when they need a tool, search comments too, and turn on AI tags:

Every post and comment then gets tags like these (a real example):

Filter the dataset on aiTags.willingToPay or aiTags.asksForRecommendation, and you have a list of people asking for what you might build. The tags are for sorting large lists, so spot-check the rows you act on.

Example: 100 posts with 50 comments each (5,000 comments) cost about $2.60, or about $7.70 with AI tags.

Yes. The scraper reads the public pages any logged-out visitor sees, so it needs no API key, OAuth app or developer account.

Reddit's Data API needs an approved app, has strict rate limits, and charges for commercial use. Self-service keys were closed in 2025. Scraping public pages avoids the approval process, and you pay only for the posts and comments you collect.

Reddit lists up to about 1,000 posts per feed or search. To go further, combine sorts and time ranges (Top of the year, Top of the month, New), or schedule runs to collect new posts over time.

#9742. I Followed the Textbook Fix for PageSpeed and My Site Got Slower

NXTO developer, build in public app that helps organize gaming

NXTO developer, build in public app that helps organize gaming

NXTO developer, build in public app that helps organize gaming

I wanted a perfect mobile PageSpeed score for my side project, a free game backlog tracker. It started at 86. Within an hour, it was 77. By the end of the afternoon, it was 99. Here is the part of that story that taught me something.

My report listed “render-blocking requests” with an estimated saving of 840 ms. The biggest blocker was the Google Fonts stylesheet. Every performance article gives the same answer: load it asynchronously.

I applied it, rebuilt, ran the test again. The score fell from 86 to 77. First Contentful Paint did not improve. Cumulative Layout Shift went from 0.001 to 0.131.

The fonts now arrived after the first paint, text rendered in a fallback font, then jumped when the real font loaded. I had not removed the cost; I had moved it from “wait” to “shift”, and the metric that punishes shifting is worth more points than I expected.

Instead of trying a third trick, I read what the tool listed under diagnostics, line by line, and checked each with curl.

1. Nothing was compressed. The report said text compression was missing. I did not believe it, because my reverse proxy config has encode gzip zstd. So I tested:

No Content-Encoding header. Not on the HTML, not on the 76 KB stylesheet.

In production, the proxy was not actually in front of the Node server. One line of Express middleware fixed it:

2. A hidden @import. A second font request appeared in the waterfall that I had never added to the page. It came from a scoped style block inside a “Buy me a coffee” button component, where someone (me, months ago) had written @import url('https://fonts.googleapis.com/...'). The bundler had merged that into the main stylesheet, so my entire CSS was waiting on a third-party server. I replaced that font with a system stack.

3. The headline was waiting for its animation. My hero used a fade-in with opacity: 0 at the start, 0.8 seconds long, with a stagger delay of up to 0.85 s. The browser cannot count an invisible element as the largest paint, so the largest contentful paint was literally behind an animation. I shortened it to 0.35 s with no stagger and a nearly-visible starting state.

With the real problems fixed, I went back to fonts and did it properly:

Accessibility also went from 95 to 100, after I raised the contrast of the footer text.

The score is a proxy. What I actually care about is that the page now appears in about a second and a half on a mid-range phone on a slow connection, and that I can explain why.

#9740. Create, Fill, Encrypt and Sign PDFs in .NET With One Free NuGet Package

Sooner or later, most business apps need PDFs. Reports and invoices have to be generated, forms filled from your data, files protected with a password, archived in a long term format, or signed before they go out.

sgcPDF .NET covers all of those jobs in one NuGet package. Everything happens in code, headless, with nothing to open on screen, so the same calls work in a console app or in a background service.

This tour has one section per task: create a document with text, a table and an image, build and fill a form, extract text and images, encrypt with AES-256, save as PDF/A-2b, and sign with PAdES B-B. Every sample was compiled against the published packages and run, and the results quoted below are what it printed.

Create a console app and add the packages:

You only need the second package for the signing sample at the end. It brings in esegece.sgcSign.Community, which supplies the signing key provider.

The packages target netstandard2.0, net472, net6.0, net8.0, net9.0 and net10.0. Through netstandard2.0 they also reach .NET Framework 4.6.2 and later, Mono and Xamarin. The samples use net8.0:

Each sample below is its own file, a static class with a Run() method, because C# allows top level statements in one file only. Drop the files into the project and call the one you want from Program.cs, for example CreateSample.Run();. Everything lives in the esegece.sgcPDF namespace, plus esegece.sgcSign for the signing key.

TsgcPDFDocument is the entry point. Add a page, draw on it and save:

Positions and sizes are in points (1/72 inch), and the origin is the bottom left corner of the page, so y grows upward. The y you pass to DrawText is the text baseline. The table is the exception: DrawOnPage takes the top left corner, and the rows grow downward from there.

The table header text is white, so give SetHeaderBackground a dark colour. A light one leaves the header row unreadable.

The sample expects a logo.png in the working directory, but any PNG, JPEG, BMP or TIFF file will do. It prints Saved 01_create.pdf, 1 page(s) and writes a 21.7 KB file. Opened again, Info.Title reads back as "Quarterly report", and the PNG is stored as a compressed image object. Here is page 1, rendered to PNG with the library's own raster renderer, TsgcPDFRendererRaster:

doc.AcroForm handles interactive forms. This sample builds a page with a text field and a check box, opens the file again to fill it, then saves a flattened copy in which the values become ordinary page content:

Two details are easy to miss. AddTextField and AddCheckBox take the two corners of the field (x1, y1, x2, y2), while DrawRectangle takes x, y, width and height. And generated fields have no visible border, which is why the sample draws a rectangle under each one, so the form reads well on screen and on paper.

The text field reads back as Ada Lovelace and the check box as Yes. In the flattened copy, AcroForm.FieldCount() returns 0 and the page text contains "Ada Lovelace", so the value is now part of the page itself. AcroForm also offers combo boxes, list boxes, radio groups, buttons and signature fields, and it exchanges field data as FDF or XFDF.

This sample reads the report from sample 1 back, the text page by page and the images as PNG files:

Use ExtractTextW, which returns Unicode text. ExtractText returns an ANSI string. The text comes back line by line, from the title through the paragraph, and the table arrives as space separated rows such as North 1,240 EUR 49,600.

The extractor finds the one image and reports it as page 1, 120 x 80, DeviceRGB. The PNG it saved was byte identical to the original logo.png. It can also save JPEG files with SaveAsJPEG, or hand you the PNG bytes in memory with GetPNGBytes.

This sample encrypts the report with a user password to open it and an owner password for full rights, and allows the user nothing but printing. Then it opens the file twice, once with the password and once without:

Use doc.Encryption.SetupEncryption with a permissions value, as above. The shorter doc.SetEncryption(method, user, owner) also encrypts, but it grants every permission, and Encryption.Permissions is read only, so you can't narrow them afterwards. Give the owner password a different value from the user password, otherwise the restrictions don't hold.

To open an encrypted file, call SetPassword before LoadFromFile. With the user password the file opens with 1 page, method emAES_256 and permissions ppPrint, ppPrintHigh, and the first line of text reads "Quarterly report". Without a password, LoadFromFile throws EsgcPDFEncryptionError with the message "Invalid password for encrypted PDF document". A wrong password throws the same error. The owner password opens the file too, with Encryption.IsOwnerPassword set to true.

In the saved bytes the encryption dictionary reads /V 5 /R 6 /CFM /AESV3, which is AES-256 at revision 6, and the title no longer appears in plain text. The other methods are emRC4_40, emRC4_128 and emAES_128.

For long term archiving, set a PDF/A level on the document, then check the saved file with the built-in validator:

PDF/A requires embedded fonts, and the standard 14 fonts are not embedded. That is why this sample registers a TrueType font with AddTrueTypeFont and draws with DrawTextTT. AddTrueTypeFont looks the font up by name among the installed system fonts, which was tested on Windows. On Linux or in a container, pass a .ttf path to AddTrueTypeFontFromFile instead.

The output is PDFALevel = paNone, valid = True, errors = 0, warnings = 0. The paNone is expected, because PDFALevel is not read back from the metadata of a loaded file. Check conformance with TsgcPDFAValidator instead. The file passes the library's own validator with no errors and no warnings. As a control, the same validator rejects the plain report from sample 1 with 7 errors, among them the missing metadata, the fonts that are not embedded and the missing output intent, so it really checks.

The saved file carries XMP metadata with PDF/A part 2 and conformance B, an sRGB output intent, the embedded font, and no encryption. Besides paA2b, TsgcPDFALevel offers paA1b, paA3b, paA1a, paA2a, paA3a, paA4 and paA4f.

Signing comes from the second package, esegece.sgcPDF.sgcSign.Community. This sample makes a self-signed test certificate in code with the BCL CertificateRequest, exports it to PFX bytes in memory, signs the report from sample 1 to PAdES B-B, and verifies the result. No certificate file touches the disk:

The verifier finds one signature and prints valid = True, subfilter = ETSI.CAdES.detached, modified = False, trusted = False. ETSI.CAdES.detached is the PAdES subfilter. The signer comes back as "Demo, sgcPDF Demo Signer", with the organization listed first.

The trusted = False is the expected result, not an error. A self-signed certificate verifies as valid and unmodified, but it isn't trusted, because no trust store knows it. In production you sign with a certificate from a trusted CA, loaded from its PFX file with key.LoadFromFile(file, password).

Verification also catches changes. In a tamper test, one byte flipped inside the signed range of a copy made VerifySignature return false.

B-B needs no network access. For B-T and above (paBT, paBLT, paBLTA), set signer.TSAURL to a time stamp server. The verifier itself is in the core package, so an app that only checks signatures needs just esegece.sgcPDF.Community.

The Community edition is free for commercial and non-commercial use by individuals and organizations under EUR 1M annual gross revenue and with no more than 5 developers. Above either threshold, a paid licence is needed. It has the same feature set as the paid editions, with no functional limits, so everything in this tour runs exactly as shown.

There is one thing you may notice. Now and then, the Community edition prints a short licence notice to stderr when the first document or parser is created. It appears at most once per process and not on every run, and most runs print nothing at all. Because it goes to stderr, output you redirect from stdout stays clean. It doesn't block: timed runs with and without the notice differed by about a millisecond.

#9739. Canva Review 2022: Details, Pricing & Features


Are you looking for a new graphic design tool? Would you like to read a detailed review of Canva? As it's one of the tools I love using. I am also writing my first ebook using canva and publish it soon on my site you can download it is free.  Let's start the review.

Canva has a web version and also a mobile app

What is Canva?

Canva is a free graphic design web application that allows you to create invitations, business cards, flyers, lesson plans, banners, and more using professionally designed templates. You can upload your own photos from your computer or from Google Drive, and add them to Canva's templates using a simple drag-and-drop interface. It's like having a basic version of Photoshop that doesn't require Graphic designing knowledge to use. It’s best for nongraphic designers.

Who is Canva best suited for?

Canva is a great tool for small business owners, online entrepreneurs, and marketers who don’t have the time and want to edit quickly.

To create sophisticated graphics, a tool such as Photoshop can is ideal. To use it, you’ll need to learn its hundreds of features, get familiar with the software, and it’s best to have a good background in design, too.

Also running the latest version of Photoshop you need a high-end computer.

So here  Canva takes place, with Canva you can do all that with drag-and-drop feature. It’s also easier to use and free. Also an even-more-affordable paid version is available for $12.95 per month.

Free vs Pro vs Enterprise Pricing plan

The product is available in three plans: Free, Pro ($12.99/month per user or  $119.99/year for up to 5 people), and Enterprise ($30 per user per month, minimum 25 people).

Free plan Features

  • 250,000+ free templates
  • 100+ design types (social media posts, presentations, letters, and more)
  • Hundreds of thousands of free photos and graphics
  • Invite members to your team
  • Collaborate and comment in real-time
  • 5GB of cloud storage
  • Try Canva Pro for free for 30 days

Pro Plan Features 

  • Everything Free, has plus:
  • 100+ million premium and  stock photos, videos, audio, and graphics
  • 610,000+ premium and free templates with new designs daily
  • Access to Background Remover and Magic Resize
  •  Create a library of your brand or campaign's colors, logos, and fonts with up to 100 Brand Kits
  • Remove image backgrounds instantly with background remover
  • Resize designs infinitely with Magic Resize
  • Save designs as templates for your team to use
  • 100GB of cloud storage
  • Schedule social media content to 8 platforms

Enterprise Plan Features

  • Everything Pro has plus:
  • Establish your brand's visual identity with logos, colors and fonts across multiple Brand Kits
  • Control your team's access to apps, graphics, logos, colors and fonts with brand controls
  • Built-in workflows to get approval on your designs
  • Set which elements your team can edit and stay on brand with template locking
  • Unlimited Storage
  • Log in with single-sign on (SSO) and have access to 24/7 Enterprise-level support.

How to Use Canva?

To get started on Canva, you will need to create an account by providing your email address, Google, Facebook or Apple credentials. You will then choose your account type between student, teacher, small business, large company, non-profit, or personal. Based on your choice of account type, templates will be recommended to you.

You can sign up for a free trial of Canva Pro, or you can start with the free version to get a sense of whether it’s the right graphic design tool for your needs.

Canva Sign Up

Designing with Canva



When you sign up for an account, Canva will suggest different post types to choose from. Based on the type of account you set up  you'll be able to see templates categorized by the following categories: social media posts, documents, presentations, marketing, events, ads, launch your business, build your online brand, etc.

 Start by choosing a template for your post or searching for something more specific. Search by social network name to see a list of post types on each network.

Templates



Next, you can choose a template. Choose from hundreds of templates that are ready to go, with customizable photos, text, and other elements.

You can start your design by choosing from a variety of ready-made templates, searching for a template matching your needs, or working with a blank template.


 Canva has a lot to choose from, so start with a specific search.if you want to create business card just search for it and you will see alot of templates to choose from

Elements

Inside the Canva designer, the Elements tab gives you access to lines and shapes, graphics, photos, videos, audio, charts, photo frames, and photo grids.The search box on the Elements tab lets you search everything on Canva.


To begin with, Canva has a large library of elements to choose from. To find them, be specific in your search query. You may also want to search in the following tabs to see various elements separately:

Photos

The Photos tab lets you search for and choose from millions of professional stock photos for your templates.

You can replace the photos in our templates to create a new look. This can also make the template more suited to your industry.

You can find photos on other stock photography sites like pexel, pixabay and many more or simply upload your own photos.


When you choose an image, Canva’s photo editing features let you adjust the photo’s settings (brightness, contrast, saturation, etc.), crop, or animate it.

 When you subscribe to Canva Pro, you get access to a number of premium features, including the Background Remover. This feature allows you to remove the background from any stock photo in  library or any image you upload.

Text

The Text tab lets you add headings, normal text, and graphical text to your design.

When you click on  text, you'll see options to adjust the font, font size, color, format, spacing, and text effects (like shadows). 

Canva Pro subscribers can choose from a large library of fonts on the Brand Kit or the Styles tab. Enterprise-level controls ensure that visual content remains on-brand, no matter how many people are working on it.

Audio

Create an animated image or video by adding audio to capture user’s attention in social news feeds.

If you want to use audio from another stock site or your own audio tracks, you can upload them in the Uploads tab or from the more option.

Video

Want to create your own videos? Choose from thousands of stock video clips. You’ll find videos that range upto 2 minutes

You can upload your own videos as well as videos from other stock sites in the Uploads tab. 

Once you have chosen a video, you can use the editing features in Canva to trim the video, flip it, and adjust its transparency.

Backgrounds

On the Background tab, you’ll find free stock photos to serve as backgrounds on your designs. Change out the background on a template to give it a more personal touch.

Styles


The Styles tab lets you quickly change the look and feel of your template with just a click. And if you have a Canva Pro subscription, you can upload your brand’s custom colors and fonts to ensure designs stay on brand.

Logos

If you have a Canva Pro subscription, you’ll have a Logos tab. Here, you can upload variations of your brand logo to use throughout your designs.

With Canva, you can also create your own logos. Note that you cannot trademark a logo with stock content in it.

Publishing with Canva

With Canva, free users can download and share designs to multiple platforms including Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Slack and Tumblr.

Canva Pro subscribers can create multiple post formats from one design. For example, you can start by designing an Instagram post, and Canva's Magic Resizer can resize it for other networks, Stories, Reels, and other formats.

Canva Pro subscribers can also use Canva’s Content Planner to post content on eight different accounts on Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Slack, and Tumblr.

Canva Team

Canva Pro allows you to work with your team on visual content. Designs can be created inside Canva, and then sent to your team members for approval. Everyone can make comments, edits, revisions, and keep track via the version history.

Canva Print

When it comes to printing your designs, Canva has you covered. With an extensive selection of printing options, they can turn your designs into anything from banners and wall art to mugs and t-shirts. 

Canva Print is perfect for any business seeking to make a lasting impression. Create inspiring designs people will want to wear, keep, and share. Hand out custom business cards that leave a lasting impression on customers' minds.

Canva Apps

The Canva app is available on the Apple App Store and Google Play. The Canva app has earned a 4.9 out of five star rating from over 946.3K Apple users and a 4.5 out of five star rating from over 6,996,708 Google users.

In addition to mobile apps, you can use Canva’s integration with other Internet services to add images and text from sources like Google Maps, Emojis, photos from Google Drive and Dropbox, YouTube videos, Flickr photos, Bitmojis, and other popular visual content elements.

Canva Pros and Cons

Pros:

  • A user-friendly interface
  • Canva is a great tool for people who want to create professional graphics but don’t have graphic design skills.
  • Hundreds of templates, so you'll never have to start from scratch.
  • Wide variety of templates to fit multiple uses
  • Branding kits to keep your team consistent with the brand colors and fonts
  • Creating visual content on the go
  • You can find royalty free images, audio, and video without having to subscribe to another service.

Cons:

  • Some professional templates are available for Pro user only
  • Advanced photo editing features like blurring or erasing a specific area are missing.
  • Some elements that fall outside of a design are tricky to retrieve.
  • Features (like Canva presentations) could use some improvement.
  • If you are a regular user of Adobe products, you might find Canva's features limited.
  • Prefers to work with vectors. Especially logos.
  • Expensive enterprise pricing

Conclusion

In general, Canva is an excellent tool for those who need simple images for projects. If you are a graphic designer with experience, you will find Canva’s platform lacking in customization and advanced features – particularly vectors. But if you have little design experience, you will find Canva easier to use than advanced graphic design tools like Adobe Photoshop or Illustrator for most projects. If you have any queries let me know in the comments section.

#9738. Building an open source subscription backend

Posted on Nov 10 • Originally published at subtru.com

My first attempt to add subscriptions to my app failed, so I built SubTru. SubTru is an open source, self-hostable API that processes subscription events from Stripe, the Apple App Store, and Google Play. Your app can then call SubTru's GET /access endpoint to fetch any user's subscription status. Below, I discuss some of the challenges I faced and the design decisions I made along the way.

I had no idea how challenging adding subscriptions to an app could be. My first attempt at this was a disaster. I had spent months writing the code to handle my users' subscriptions, but all it took was one small misconfiguration for things to break. Long story short, my logic didn't update my customer's subscription status after they made a purchase. I was able to quickly fix the problem, but I felt horrible that I had failed my customer. I felt so bad about the situation, that I vowed to build the most bulletproof subscription handling infrastructure possible and make it open source, so this wouldn't have to happen to anyone else.

Subscription handling is complicated. Providers like Stripe, the Apple App Store and Google Play send out events (webhooks or real-time developer notifications in Google's case) whenever your users purchase or change their subscriptions. Those events need to be processed to create and maintain an accurate record of your users' subscriptions. It sounds simple enough on the surface, but here are a few challenges I faced:

There were four main requirements I had in mind for the subscription handling infrastructure I wanted to build.

These requirements helped me narrow down the possible designs for the infrastructure, but even still, I could have built things in a variety of ways without any of them being "wrong". With most system design problems, they are nuanced and come down to the advantages and tradeoffs unique to your situation.

Since this service would need to receive subscription events from providers and also make user subscription data available to external apps, it made sense to design part of it as an API. I added an HTTP POST /webhooks endpoint for each provider to send events to, and a GET /access endpoint for apps to fetch user subscription access data. This service would also need to process those provider events and store user subscription data somewhere. Trying to pick the "right" design for event processing was challenging because there were so many ways to combine or split functionality between different services. After weighing the pros and cons around things like failure isolation, failure recovery, scalability, and deployment simplicity, I decided to use a single service to receive and process events. I've considered adding a queue for incoming events so they can be processed separately from when they are received, but there isn't a clear need for that at the moment since the system isn't bottlenecked, and providers can resend events that failed to process. The current approach also has much less complexity for deployment and maintainability.

The database decision wasn't as crucial. Since the service just needs a place to store and read data, both a relational or NoSQL DB could have been used here. I decided to go with Postgres since a lot of the data we store is relational in nature, and Postgres is widely adopted by the open source community.

I try to use serverless functions when they make sense, because I like that they eliminate idle compute costs, but they also have some drawbacks like cold starts, setup complexity, and less support outside AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud. For those reasons, and given our requirements, I figured a containerized service on a long-lived machine made more sense. I added a Dockerfile in the GitHub repo so self-hosters can easily deploy the Docker image to their hosting platform of choice. It also doesn't stop self-hosters from deploying to serverless container platforms if they prefer. I've also provided SQL migration scripts in the repo so self-hosters can quickly set up their Postgres database.

Now, whenever I need to add subscription handling to an app, I don't have to spend months rewriting everything from scratch. All I have to do is deploy the service from the Docker image, run the migration scripts to set up the database, and configure my subscription providers (Stripe, the Apple App Store, and/or Google Play) to send events to the API. Once that's done, I can call the GET /access endpoint from my app whenever I need to fetch a user's subscription status.

My app then uses the productId and hasAccess values to decide what features my user has access to. I can optionally cache the customer's subscription status for a duration so I don't have to make repeated calls to the API.

This project is called SubTru. Here's a link to the homepage if you want to learn more. SubTru is completely open source under the Apache 2.0 license, and all contributions are greatly appreciated. There is also a managed, SubTru Cloud offering with a dashboard if you would rather not self-host.

Thank you so much for your time. I know it's valuable, so I don't take it for granted. Let me know what you think about SubTru so I can learn what's going right and what could be better!

Please consider giving SubTru a star on GitHub. It would mean the world to me.

What's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Your net worth is the single most important number in personal finance. Not your salary. Not your credit score. Not how much you have in checking. Your net worth — the gap between everything you own and everything you owe — tells you exactly where you stand financially and whether you are moving in the right direction.

Net Worth = Total Assets - Total Liabilities

That is it. Add up everything you own that has monetary value. Subtract everything you owe. The number that remains — positive or negative — is your net worth.

In the FI community, net worth is not just a number. It is the scoreboard. Your FI number (25 times your annual spending) is a net worth target. Every dollar you save and invest moves you closer. Every dollar of debt you pay off does the same. Tracking your net worth turns the abstract concept of "financial independence" into a concrete, measurable goal.

Let's walk through exactly how to calculate yours, what counts as an asset, what counts as a liability, and how to use this number to accelerate your path to FI.

Calculating your net worth requires two lists: everything you own (assets) and everything you owe (liabilities). The difference between these two numbers is your net worth.

An asset is anything you own that has monetary value. Be honest and conservative — list items at what they would actually sell for today, not what you paid for them or what you hope they are worth.

A note on your home: The FI community debates whether to include your primary residence in net worth calculations. The pragmatic approach is to include it but recognize it is an illiquid asset that does not generate income. For FI planning purposes, many people track two numbers: total net worth (including home equity) and investable net worth (excluding home equity). Your investable net worth is what actually funds your financial independence.

A liability is any debt or financial obligation you owe to someone else.

A surgeon earning $400,000 per year with $600,000 in student loans, a $1.2 million mortgage, and $50,000 in car loans might have a lower net worth than a teacher earning $55,000 who has been investing 30% of her salary into index funds for 15 years. Income is what flows in. Net worth is what you keep. The FI community learned this lesson early: it is not about how much you earn — it is about the gap between earning and spending, compounded over time.

Let's walk through a real example. Meet Sarah, a 32-year-old software developer earning $95,000 per year. She has been saving and investing for 5 years since paying off her credit cards.

Sarah's net worth is $140,700. If her annual spending is $45,000, her FI number is $1,125,000 (25 x $45,000). She is 12.5% of the way there. More importantly, she is tracking her number every month and watching it grow — which means she can project when she will reach FI and make strategic decisions about how to accelerate the timeline.

Her investable net worth (excluding the car, which depreciates) is $155,200 - $30,500 = $124,700 in productive financial assets. This is the number that matters most for FI planning.

ChooseFI has partnered with CardRatings for our coverage of credit card products. ChooseFI and CardRatings may receive a commission from card issuers.

A negative net worth means you owe more than you own. This is completely normal — and far more common than people realize. According to Federal Reserve data, the median net worth for Americans under 35 is $39,000, but this is skewed by homeowners. For young renters with student loans, a negative net worth in the range of -$20,000 to -$80,000 is typical.

A negative net worth does not mean you are failing. It means you are early in the journey. If you graduated with $80,000 in student loans and have $5,000 in savings, your net worth is -$75,000. But if you are earning income, paying down debt, and starting to invest, your trajectory is positive — and trajectory is what matters.

The FI community is full of people who started with six-figure negative net worths and reached financial independence in 10-15 years. The key was tracking the number, seeing the progress, and letting that momentum fuel consistent action.

Calculating your net worth once is useful. Tracking it monthly is transformational. Monthly tracking turns financial independence from an abstract goal into a visible, measurable trajectory.

The FI community's favorite: Many FI practitioners use a simple spreadsheet. Create columns for each account, update balances on the first of every month, and chart the total over time. The visual of a steadily rising line graph is one of the most powerful motivators on the FI path. Some people prefer Empower for automated tracking — it links to your accounts and updates your net worth in real time.

Your net worth will not increase in a straight line. Market drops will temporarily reduce your investment balances. Large purchases (a car, a home down payment) will create short-term dips. The number to watch is the 12-month trend. If your net worth is higher than it was a year ago, you are moving in the right direction.

Early in the journey, debt payoff drives most of the growth. A $30,000 student loan shrinking to $18,000 adds $12,000 to your net worth just as effectively as saving $12,000 in new investments. Later, compound growth takes over and your net worth starts increasing faster than your contributions — that is the magic inflection point where your money starts working harder than you do.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Complete this in one sitting — it takes about 30 minutes.

Log into every bank account, retirement account, brokerage account, and HSA. Write down the current balance. For your home, use Zillow's estimate minus 10%. For vehicles, use Kelley Blue Book private party value.

Pro tip: Do not include personal belongings like furniture, clothing, or electronics unless a single item is worth more than $1,000 at resale.

Log into every loan servicer, credit card account, and any other creditor. Write down the exact payoff balance — not the monthly payment, but the total remaining balance including any accrued interest.

Total assets minus total liabilities equals your net worth. Whether this number is positive, negative, or zero, write it down. This is your starting point.

Multiply your annual spending by 25. This is how much investable net worth you need to be financially independent using the 4% safe withdrawal rate. Divide your current investable net worth by your FI number to see your progress percentage.

Pro tip: Use your actual spending, not your income. If you earn $80,000 but spend $50,000, your FI number is $1,250,000 — not $2,000,000.

Choose a tool — Empower, a spreadsheet, or a notebook — and schedule a recurring monthly reminder to update your net worth. The first of each month works well. Track the number, chart the trend, and watch your progress compound.

The most common habit among people who have reached financial independence is consistent net worth tracking. It takes 5 minutes per month and creates a feedback loop that keeps you motivated and accountable. When you see your net worth climb from $50,000 to $100,000 to $250,000, the progress becomes its own fuel. Start tracking today — your future self will thank you.

Yes, but with context. Your home is an asset and your mortgage is a liability, so both should be included for an accurate net worth picture. However, for FI planning, track your investable net worth (excluding home equity) separately — because you cannot live off your home equity unless you sell or take a reverse mortgage. Many FI practitioners track both numbers.

Monthly is the sweet spot for most people. Weekly is too frequent and causes unnecessary anxiety about market fluctuations. Quarterly is too infrequent to maintain the motivational feedback loop. Set a recurring reminder on the first of each month, update your numbers in 5 minutes, and move on.

The median net worth by age (from Federal Reserve SCF data): under 35 is $39,000, 35-44 is $135,600, 45-54 is $247,200, 55-64 is $364,500, 65-74 is $409,900. FI community members typically far exceed these benchmarks because they prioritize saving and investing. See our average net worth by age guide for detailed breakdowns.

Yes. Your 401(k), IRA, Roth IRA, 403(b), TSP, and any other retirement accounts are assets and should be included in your net worth calculation. Some people adjust for taxes (since traditional 401(k) withdrawals are taxed as income), but for tracking purposes, including the full balance is standard practice.

A negative net worth simply means you owe more than you own — it is common for recent graduates, new homeowners, and anyone early in their career. What matters is the direction. If your net worth is -$50,000 but was -$65,000 a year ago, you are making significant progress. Focus on the trajectory, not the absolute number.

Yes, include your car at its current resale value (Kelley Blue Book private party value, not dealer retail). Cars are depreciating assets, which means their value decreases over time, but they still have monetary value and should be counted. If you have an auto loan, both the car (asset) and the loan balance (liability) should appear in your calculation.

Calculating your net worth is the first step on the path to financial independence — and it takes less than 30 minutes. Add up everything you own, subtract everything you owe, and you have the single most important number in your financial life. Whether that number is positive, negative, or zero, it is your starting point. Track it monthly, watch it grow, and use it to measure your progress toward your FI number. The formula is simple: assets minus liabilities. The habit of tracking it is what separates people who talk about financial goals from people who achieve them.
